small_guidance:
- Add larger-tile autotune configs targeted at this shape (M=N=K=8192): try `BLOCK_M=128, BLOCK_N=256, BLOCK_K=64, num_warps=8, num_stages=3/4` and `BLOCK_M=256, BLOCK_N=128, BLOCK_K=32, num_warps=8, num_stages=4`. Since M/N/K are all multiples of 256, drop the mask on the K-loop loads (pass `boundary_check=()` style — load without masks) and only mask the epilogue store; this removes per-iteration mask overhead.
- Switch to fp16/bf16 (or tf32) accumulation path: cast `A`/`Wt` to bf16 on entry (kept as fp32 master) or call `tl.dot(a, b, allow_tf32=True)`; on Ada/4090 TF32/BF16 tensor cores deliver ~2× the throughput of fp32 dot. Verify under the 5e-2 tolerance.
- Pre-transpose weight once in `__init__` (not lazily) and store as a buffer so `_get_wt` is free; also store bias on CUDA at init to remove the per-call `.cuda()`/`.contiguous()` checks.
large_guidance:
- Rewrite as a split-K or stream-K GEMM: K=8192 is large and a single program reducing the entire K serializes on one SM tile; split-K (e.g., SPLIT_K=2 or 4 with atomic-add or a small post-reduction kernel that also fuses scale+hardtanh+GELU) lets more SMs participate. Apply the epilogue (scale, hardtanh, GELU) only in the final reduction kernel.
- Use bf16 inputs with fp32 accumulators end-to-end: store the transposed weight as bf16 in init, cast activations to bf16 on entry, do `tl.dot` with bf16 operands. This roughly halves DRAM traffic for the K-loop and uses the BF16 tensor cores on the 4090 — the dominant win at this size.
- Consider a persistent-kernel design (one program per SM, looping over output tiles) to amortize launch and improve L2 reuse of the weight tiles across the 16×64 output tile grid; combined with GROUP_M swizzle this commonly buys 10–20% on square 8192³ GEMMs.
